title: Why's that dude in that dumpster?
summary: Josh and Chuck open with a plug for Kiva, the microlending team, then explore the trademark problem of "genericized" brand names (Xerox, Dumpster, Realtor, band-aid, etc.) and the origin of the Dempster Dumpster. They turn to freegans, people who reclaim discarded food and goods and reject consumerism, covering urban foraging, dumpster diving, the Supreme Court's California v. Greenwood ruling, the Good Samaritan food donation act, date labels on food, gleaning, the Diggers and Keith McHenry, Food Not Bombs, time banks, and an Australian freegan example. The episode closes with a listener mail about zebra fish in a neuroscience lab.
topics: Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Food Donation Act

segments.title: Opening and Kiva plug
segments.summary: Hosts greet listeners and promote the Kiva lending team, noting the team reached about 400,000 dollars in loans made to entrepreneurs in developing countries, with a 25-dollar minimum loan that gets repaid.

segments.title: Genericized trademarks
segments.summary: Discussion of Xerox asking people to say photocopy, and how brand names like aspirin, escalator, trampoline, zipper, and yo-yo became generic. Other examples include Jacuzzi, Kleenex, Crock-Pot, Rolodex, Ping-Pong, and Skivvies, and the distinction that a realtor is a specific company's agent. Band-Aid changed its jingle to avoid genericizing.

segments.title: Origin of the Dumpster
segments.summary: The dumpster was invented by George Dempster, later mayor of Knoxville, Tennessee, who wanted a receptacle that could be hoisted into a dump truck. His wife reportedly vetoed the name Dempster Dumpster, and the trademarked term became Dumpster. Hosts note waste companies often use owners' names.

segments.title: What freegans are
segments.summary: Introduction to freegans, who are also called post-consumerists or reclaimists. They are anti-consumerism, scavenge and reclaim goods, volunteer, squat, and avoid paid work. Freegans differ from homeless people because they choose this life and usually could afford food. The hosts note that the name is a blend of free and vegan, and that Keith McHenry is described as the movement's founder.

segments.title: Food waste and freegan philosophy
segments.summary: Hosts cite estimates that the US wastes roughly 96 billion pounds of food a year, including bruised or mashed food. They discuss virtual water and the energy lost in wasted food. Freegans eat food they find and aim to shame wasteful consumers. Critics call freegans hypocrites for using gas and electricity. The hosts discuss hitchhiking and freeloading, and the freegan rejection of upgrades and paid jobs.

segments.title: Urban foraging, New York, and the law
segments.summary: Freegans volunteer, work for causes, and repair items; time banks let volunteers earn time dollars. Hosts describe New York City trash day and urban foraging for furniture, clothes, and electronics. The Supreme Court case California v. Greenwood ruled that trash put on the curb is public property. Many cities have anti-scavenging laws, and some stores lock or cage dumpsters.

segments.title: Good Samaritan food donation and date labels
segments.summary: The Bill Emerson Good Samaritan Act protects people who donate or handle food for the poor from liability, if they are not acting in bad faith. Hosts explain that US food dating is voluntary except for baby formula and baby food, that the use-by date is the one to respect, and that eggs and some sealed bacon can remain good past their sell-by dates. They also discuss the smell test and safe food temperatures.

segments.title: Gleaning, Diggers, Food Not Bombs, and Daniel Zeta
segments.summary: Gleaning is the biblical practice of collecting leftover crops after harvest, now done by groups such as the Society of St Andrew. Freeganism traces roots to Gerrard Winstanley and the Diggers of 1649 England, and to Keith McHenry, Food Not Bombs, and Homes not Jails. The hosts describe Daniel Zeta, an American who moved to Tasmania, quit a government job, and lives on about 200 dollars a month by trading work for food and lodging.

segments.title: Freegan healthcare and wrap-up
segments.summary: The hosts mention freegan healthcare collectives and free clinics, and a freegan marketplace for bartering. They point listeners to the freegan website and the How Stuff Works search bar for more information and to a related episode about how much money a person needs to live.

segments.title: Zebra fish listener mail
segments.summary: Alex, a neuroscience lab technician studying sleep and circadian rhythms in zebra fish, writes that the fish react to the podcast and asks the hosts to acknowledge the fish's hard work in cocaine experiments. The hosts joke about it.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Closing remarks and the sponsor line, with an invitation to send odd experiments to the show's email.
